aestheticism: Aestheticism is the view that beauty and artistic value matter in their own right, apart from moral, religious, or practical worth — the creed of 'art for art's sake.' On this view the aesthete takes aesthetic experience, not ethics or utility, as the highest measure of life. Some hold it to its extreme: that art needs no justification beyond the pleasure of contemplating it.
anti-natalism: Anti-natalism is the view that it is morally wrong to bring new people into existence. Its defenders, such as David Benatar, argue that every life contains real suffering, while the nonexistent cannot be deprived of pleasure, so creating someone always harms them — or at least imposes on them risks they never consented to. On this view, adopting existing children is morally preferable to procreation.
art-horror: 'Art-horror' is philosopher Noël Carroll's term for the distinctive emotion aroused by horror fiction: a blend of fear and disgust aimed at monsters. He holds that horror monsters characteristically violate our cultural categories — fusions of species, mixtures of living and dead, formless or incomplete things. This 'categorical impurity' is why revulsion and fascination typically arrive together.
bergson-duration: For Henri Bergson, 'duration' (durée) is time as we actually live it: a continuous, flowing, qualitative stream in which past and present interpenetrate. It contrasts with clock time, which cuts experience into countable, spatialized units. Bergson held that science measures clock time but only intuition can grasp duration — the medium in which life and creativity unfold.
bergson-memory: In Matter and Memory, Bergson argued that memory is not a storehouse of images kept in the brain but the past actively surviving into every present perception. What we perceive is already interlaced with what we remember. He distinguished habit-memory — learned repetition — from true memory of the unique past, and held that mind and matter meet in lived action rather than in a detached inner theater.
corporate-personhood: Corporate personhood is the idea that a corporation can count as a 'person' — holding rights, entering contracts, and bearing responsibility — even though it is not a human being. Legal systems grant this status by law, and some philosophers argue corporations can also be moral agents whose decisions and responsibilities are not reducible to any individual's. Others insist the label is a fiction that lets real people escape blame.
dharma: In Indian traditions, dharma names both the cosmic order that holds the world together and the duties appropriate to each person's station and role. The Bhagavad Gita's famous teaching is to perform one's own duty without attachment to its rewards. What counts as right action thus depends not only on universal rules but on who and where you are.
disability-philosophy: The philosophy of disability asks what disability is and what it means for a life. Many philosophers distinguish a medical model, which locates disability in the body as a defect to be cured, from a social model, which locates it in environments built for typical bodies. Debates continue over whether disability itself is a harm, a mere difference, or sometimes a gain.
gnosticism: Gnosticism was a family of early religious movements holding that salvation comes through gnosis — direct inner knowledge of the divine — rather than faith, ritual, or church. Many Gnostics taught that the material world was made not by the true God but by a lesser, flawed creator, leaving sparks of the divine trapped in matter and waiting to be awakened.
great-chain-of-being: The Great Chain of Being was the premodern picture of reality as a single ranked hierarchy: God at the top, then angels, humans, animals, plants, and inert matter, each thing with its fixed place. It implied that some beings are naturally higher than others. Evolutionary thinking is widely held to have dissolved the chain — species form a branching tree, not a ladder.
imaginative-resistance: Imaginative resistance is a puzzle about fiction: readers easily imagine impossible physics — faster-than-light travel, flying pigs — yet balk at imagining a world where morality itself is different, such as a story where cold-blooded murder is noble. Many hold that we simply refuse to 'enter into' vicious sentiments, even in imagination. Explaining exactly why we resist, and when, remains debated.
intentional-stance: The intentional stance is Daniel Dennett's proposal that we understand and predict a system's behavior by treating it as if it had beliefs and desires. We adopt this stance toward other people, but also toward thermostats and chess computers. It is a predictive strategy, not necessarily a claim about what really goes on inside — though Dennett holds that the patterns found this way can still be fully real.
intersectionality: Intersectionality, coined by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, is the idea that systems of oppression — racism, sexism, classism — do not operate separately but intersect, producing forms of disadvantage unique to their overlap. A Black woman, for example, can face treatment that is neither racism as men experience it nor sexism as white women experience it. The term also names the broader practice of analyzing identity this way.
neoplatonism: Neoplatonism is the late-antique philosophy of Plotinus and his followers, built around 'the One': a supreme source beyond all being, thought, and description. From the One, reality flows outward in levels — Intellect, Soul, and finally the material world — like light from a sun. The soul's task is to turn inward and upward, returning toward its source.
personhood: In philosophy, personhood is the status of being a being to whom moral consideration is owed — standardly tied to capacities like self-consciousness, rationality, and the ability to see oneself as persisting over time. Many philosophers argue that personhood and biological humanity can come apart: some humans might lack it, and some non-human or artificial beings might have it. Whether that argument succeeds is deeply contested.
political-realism: Political realism is the view that politics is governed above all by power, interest, and the need for order — not by moral ideals. Realists from Machiavelli onward have argued that a ruler who insists on doing only what is morally admirable may lose everything worth protecting. Compromise, deception, and force, on this view, are often not corruptions of politics but its ordinary materials.
schopenhauer-pendulum: Arthur Schopenhauer described life as a pendulum swinging between pain and boredom. Wanting something we lack feels like suffering; the moment we get it, the want vanishes and emptiness sets in, driving new desires. Behind the cycle he placed the 'will' — a blind, restless striving he took to be the essence of all life — which is why his philosophy is famously pessimistic.
simulation-hypothesis: The simulation hypothesis holds that our world may be a computer simulation run by a technologically advanced civilization. Philosopher Nick Bostrom argues that if such civilizations typically create many simulated minds, most minds like ours would be simulated, making it statistically likely that we are too. The idea descends from older skeptical scenarios such as Descartes' deceiving demon and the 'brain in a vat.'
spinoza-conatus: For Spinoza, conatus is the striving of every thing to persist in its own being. This effort is not something a creature has added on; it simply is its essence — what it is to be that thing, considered as active. Human desire, on his account, is this same striving experienced consciously, and giving up on life means being overcome by causes stronger than one's own nature.
spinoza-determinism: Spinoza taught strict necessity: everything that happens follows from the nature of God — which he identified with Nature itself — as inevitably as a conclusion follows from its premises. Nothing is contingent, and nothing could have been otherwise. Freedom, on this view, is not escaping causation but understanding it: acting from one's own nature while grasping why things must be as they are.
subjective-truth: 'Subjectivity is truth' is Kierkegaard's slogan for the claim that the deepest truths are not neutral facts one observes but truths one lives. What matters most for existence — faith, how to live, what death means — is grasped only through passionate personal commitment, not detached evidence-gathering. He did not deny objective facts; he held that the truths most vital to a self require inward appropriation.
tragedy-of-the-commons: The tragedy of the commons describes how a shared resource gets ruined by individually rational behavior: each herder benefits fully from adding one more animal, while the cost of overgrazing is spread across everyone. Multiply that by many users and the common pasture is destroyed — even though no one wanted that outcome. The phrase, from Garrett Hardin, now names this whole family of collective-action problems.
transcendentalism: Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century American movement, led by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau, holding that each person carries an inner light connecting them directly to nature and the divine. It prized self-reliance, intuition, and the natural world over institutions, traditions, and inherited creeds. Its essays remain touchstones for the ideal of a life lived from one's own center.
zhuangzi-perspectivism: Zhuangzi, a fourth-century BCE Daoist thinker, is famous for the butterfly dream: he dreamed he was a butterfly, woke, and wondered whether he was a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming it is a man. The story captures his perspectivism — that no single vantage point fixes what is real — and his ease with transformation, fluid identity, and letting go of rigid categories.
